questions.stem: Which resource does CLZ-270's Azure Monitor autoscale setting target?

options.A: The load balancer's public IP only
options.B: The local terraform.tfvars file
options.C: The administrator's workstation CPU
options.D: The VMSS ID exposed by the shared windows-iis-vmss module

optionExplanations.A: The public IP does not provide the scalable VM instance capacity.
optionExplanations.B: Azure Monitor does not scale a local file.
optionExplanations.C: The metric target is the deployed Azure VMSS.
optionExplanations.D: The policy references module.windows_iis_vmss.vmss_id.

questions.stem: Which capacity relationship does the lesson validate?

options.A: maximum <= default <= minimum
options.B: minimum <= default <= maximum
options.C: minimum must always equal maximum
options.D: default must be zero in every autoscale profile

optionExplanations.A: That reverses the intended lower and upper bounds.
optionExplanations.B: The object must have ordered whole-number bounds.
optionExplanations.C: The lesson permits a range for scaling.
optionExplanations.D: The lesson validates capacities from one through five.

questions.stem: A learner supplies { minimum = 3, default = 2, maximum = 4 }. Why does validation fail?

options.A: The maximum must be below two
options.B: All capacities must be different
options.C: Azure requires capacity values to be private IP addresses
options.D: The default capacity is below the requested minimum

optionExplanations.A: Four is within the lesson's allowed range.
optionExplanations.B: Equal or distinct values can both satisfy the ordering.
optionExplanations.C: Capacity values represent instance counts.
optionExplanations.D: The ordered object contract prevents inconsistent desired capacity.

questions.stem: Which capacity object is valid under CLZ-270's lesson constraints?

options.A: { minimum = 1, default = 2.5, maximum = 4 }
options.B: { minimum = 3, default = 2, maximum = 4 }
options.C: { minimum = 1, default = 2, maximum = 4 }
options.D: { minimum = 1, default = 2, maximum = 6 }

optionExplanations.A: The default is fractional.
optionExplanations.B: The default is below the minimum.
optionExplanations.C: These are bounded whole numbers with the required ordering.
optionExplanations.D: The maximum exceeds the lesson's limit of five.

questions.stem: The observed aggregated CPU is exactly 70 percent. Does the declared GreaterThan 70 rule alone match?

options.A: No; its comparison requires CPU above 70
options.B: Yes; GreaterThan means greater than or equal
options.C: Yes; the frontend port 80 makes every CPU threshold inclusive
options.D: No; because Azure Monitor cannot read CPU metrics

optionExplanations.A: The configured operator is strict GreaterThan.
optionExplanations.B: The comparison does not include equality.
optionExplanations.C: Network ports do not redefine operators.
optionExplanations.D: CPU is the declared metric.

questions.stem: Which aggregated CPU condition can satisfy the lesson's scale-in metric rule?

options.A: CPU above 70 percent
options.B: CPU exactly 25 percent under the strict LessThan operator
options.C: Any CPU value whenever HTTP succeeds
options.D: CPU below 25 percent

optionExplanations.A: That is the scale-out condition.
optionExplanations.B: Equality does not satisfy a strict comparison.
optionExplanations.C: HTTP success is not this CPU trigger.
optionExplanations.D: The rule uses LessThan with threshold 25.

questions.stem: How much metric history does each CLZ-270 rule evaluate for its CPU threshold?

options.A: Only the last browser request
options.B: A one-month invoice average
options.C: A five-minute window with Average aggregation
options.D: Exactly one second of peak CPU

optionExplanations.A: Browser traffic is not the direct metric sample.
optionExplanations.B: The rule evaluates CPU history, not billing.
optionExplanations.C: The configuration declares time_window PT5M and time_aggregation Average.
optionExplanations.D: The declared window and aggregation do not match that.

questions.stem: The metric trigger has time_grain = PT1M and time_window = PT5M. What does that mean?

options.A: One-minute metric granularity is considered over the five-minute evaluation window
options.B: The rule adds five instances every minute
options.C: The scale set is destroyed after five minutes
options.D: Every IIS request must last one minute

optionExplanations.A: The fields represent sample granularity and evaluation duration.
optionExplanations.B: Capacity actions and metric time fields are separate.
optionExplanations.C: No timed destroy action is declared.
optionExplanations.D: Metric grain does not impose request duration.

questions.stem: Why do CLZ-270's actions have a five-minute cooldown?

options.A: To stop all HTTP delivery for five minutes
options.B: To let a scaling action take effect before additional scaling decisions
options.C: To guarantee every VM has finished Windows updates
options.D: To delay Terraform state deletion

optionExplanations.A: Cooldown is not an outage instruction.
optionExplanations.B: Cooldown limits reactions while capacity and load redistribute.
optionExplanations.C: It does not prove guest patch completion.
optionExplanations.D: Autoscale cooldown is unrelated to local state cleanup.

questions.stem: When an eligible scale-out action executes within the bounds, what does ChangeCount value 1 request?

options.A: Double the current fleet
options.B: Set capacity permanently to one
options.C: Add one instance
options.D: Increase every VM's CPU count by one

optionExplanations.A: Doubling would not be ChangeCount 1.
optionExplanations.B: The action changes by one rather than setting capacity to one.
optionExplanations.C: The action is Increase by an absolute count of one.
optionExplanations.D: It scales instance count, not VM SKU.

questions.stem: CPU remains high while the scale set already has its configured maximum capacity. What should the learner expect from this policy?

options.A: The policy ignores the maximum under load
options.B: No scale-out beyond the maximum solely because CPU stays high
options.C: The load balancer automatically creates another subscription
options.D: Terraform removes the maximum from the input file

optionExplanations.A: High load does not nullify the upper bound.
optionExplanations.B: The capacity profile limits automatic instance growth.
optionExplanations.C: There is no such capacity mechanism.
optionExplanations.D: Azure Monitor does not edit local Terraform inputs.

questions.stem: The fleet has reached its configured minimum and CPU remains low. What limit applies?

options.A: The policy deletes all instances because CPU is low
options.B: The public IP enforces a minimum of zero
options.C: The Windows username determines the next instance count
options.D: The policy should not reduce instance count below the minimum

optionExplanations.A: The minimum remains an active bound.
optionExplanations.B: The public IP does not define autoscale capacity.
optionExplanations.C: Guest identity is unrelated to the scaling bound.
optionExplanations.D: The lower bound protects the chosen baseline capacity.

questions.stem: Which autoscale object value does CLZ-270 initially pass to the shared VMSS module as instance_count?

options.A: default
options.B: maximum unconditionally
options.C: minimum minus one
options.D: The average of the two CPU thresholds

optionExplanations.A: The root module uses autoscale_capacity.default for its desired initial capacity.
optionExplanations.B: The module input is not always the upper bound.
optionExplanations.C: The code does not subtract from the minimum.
optionExplanations.D: CPU threshold arithmetic is not the capacity input.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish capacity bounds from monetary limits
questions.stem: Does maximum = 4 guarantee that the Azure bill cannot exceed a fixed currency amount?

options.A: No; it caps this policy's instance count, while other charges and usage still vary
options.B: Yes; it guarantees the monthly bill is four dollars
options.C: Yes; the autoscale setting cancels all storage charges
options.D: No; because the maximum is ignored in every deployment

optionExplanations.A: A capacity limit is not a spending-limit enforcement service.
optionExplanations.B: Instance count is not a currency value.
optionExplanations.C: It does not remove managed disks or other service costs.
optionExplanations.D: The bound is meaningful for capacity, just not a monetary guarantee.

questions.stem: Which capacity should the learner consider when checking regional quota before deploying CLZ-270?

options.A: Only minimum because extra instances are free
options.B: Only the number of public IPs
options.C: The count of local Markdown files
options.D: The configured maximum, not only the initial default

optionExplanations.A: Additional instances consume compute quota and cost.
optionExplanations.B: The frontend IP count does not measure VM quota.
optionExplanations.C: Documentation files are not Azure VM capacity.
optionExplanations.D: Automatic growth must fit available quota and budget headroom.

questions.stem: A short CPU spike does not immediately add an instance. What should be examined first?

options.A: Whether the Role tag is uppercase
options.B: The metric window, aggregation, cooldown, and autoscale history
options.C: Whether the public IP hostname contains the word autoscale
options.D: Whether the learner clicked the site theme toggle

optionExplanations.A: The rule does not use Role casing.
optionExplanations.B: These mechanisms intentionally avoid reacting to every transient sample.
optionExplanations.C: Naming does not activate the metric trigger.
optionExplanations.D: Browser styling does not affect Azure scaling.

questions.stem: Autoscale is enabled, but the relevant CPU metric stream has no usable data. What conclusion is appropriate?

options.A: The system treats missing data as 100-percent CPU automatically
options.B: The setting automatically loads CPU data from the Terraform state file
options.C: The configured threshold alone does not prove that scaling should already occur
options.D: Missing metrics disable all NSG rules

optionExplanations.A: That is not the lesson's assumed behavior.
optionExplanations.B: Terraform state is not the live metric stream.
optionExplanations.C: Diagnose metric availability and the rule's target before judging capacity behavior.
optionExplanations.D: Metric absence does not change network policy.

questions.stem: To demonstrate both bounded CPU autoscaling configuration and usable web delivery, which evidence should the learner collect?

options.A: Only VMSS capacity at one instant, without reviewing the policy
options.B: The policy shows the intended bounds and two rules, and the frontend returns the expected HTTP response
options.C: Only one successful CPU sample with no policy inspection
options.D: Only an enabled action group, without a policy or endpoint check

optionExplanations.A: A capacity snapshot does not confirm the bounds, rule definitions, or application readiness.
optionExplanations.B: Both control-plane policy and data-plane delivery need verification.
optionExplanations.C: That cannot confirm configured bounds and rule definitions.
optionExplanations.D: An action group does not prove the autoscale policy or web delivery path.

questions.stem: The lesson deliberately plans an invalid ordering { minimum = 3, default = 2, maximum = 1 }. What should happen?

options.A: Input validation rejects the plan without applying Azure changes
options.B: Azure deletes every running instance immediately
options.C: Terraform silently swaps minimum and maximum
options.D: The policy accepts the object because all values are integers

optionExplanations.A: The exercise proves the guardrail through a nonapplying command.
optionExplanations.B: The plan does not execute resource changes.
optionExplanations.C: The validator rejects instead of repairing the user's values.
optionExplanations.D: Both whole-number and ordering constraints must hold.

questions.learningObjective: Avoid assuming new capacity is instantly useful
questions.stem: Autoscale adds an instance, but HTTP delivery capacity has not increased immediately. What is a likely factor?

options.A: The frontend must receive a new public IP for every instance
options.B: The local quiz must be graded before Azure sends traffic
options.C: The new instance needs provisioning, guest bootstrap, and healthy probe status
options.D: Scale-out can only add private DNS zones

optionExplanations.A: A stable frontend can serve a growing backend pool.
optionExplanations.B: Browser assessments do not gate Azure networking.
optionExplanations.C: Added compute must become application-ready before receiving useful traffic.
optionExplanations.D: It adds VMSS instances in this lesson.

questions.stem: Why use scale-out above 70 percent and scale-in below 25 percent instead of identical CPU thresholds?

options.A: The gap encrypts metric samples
options.B: Azure requires exactly those two percentages for all workloads
options.C: The gap reserves 45 new public IPs
options.D: The gap helps reduce repeated opposing reactions near one boundary

optionExplanations.A: Threshold selection does not encrypt metrics.
optionExplanations.B: They are this lesson's choices, not universal required values.
optionExplanations.C: It has no public-IP allocation meaning.
optionExplanations.D: Distinct thresholds and cooldown support steadier capacity behavior.

questions.stem: A production queue worker has growing queue depth while CPU remains low. What change should be considered?

options.A: Use a demand metric such as queue depth if it better represents required capacity
options.B: Assume low CPU proves no queued work exists
options.C: Increase the page-message length to simulate CPU demand
options.D: Remove the maximum so all quota is consumed automatically

optionExplanations.A: CPU is not always the best signal for application demand.
optionExplanations.B: A backlog can exist with low CPU for other reasons.
optionExplanations.C: Page text is not a reliable queue metric.
optionExplanations.D: Unbounded growth does not fix metric selection.

questions.stem: Which action describes CLZ-270's autoscaling?

options.A: Replacing Standard_B2s with a larger SKU whenever CPU rises
options.B: Changing the number of VMSS instances
options.C: Adding one CPU core inside the same VM after each request
options.D: Moving the workload to a new region automatically

optionExplanations.A: That is vertical scaling and is not this rule action.
optionExplanations.B: The rules adjust capacity using ChangeCount.
optionExplanations.C: The action does not alter guest cores directly.
optionExplanations.D: This policy targets one existing scale set.

questions.stem: Which evidence best connects a load test to a scaling decision?

options.A: Only the number of browser refreshes
options.B: Only the color of the VMSS icon
options.C: Time-aligned demand, CPU metrics, autoscale history, and instance readiness
options.D: Only an unchanged Terraform lockfile

optionExplanations.A: Refresh count alone does not describe aggregated CPU or actions.
optionExplanations.B: An icon is not operational evidence.
optionExplanations.C: These signals explain trigger conditions and useful capacity.
optionExplanations.D: Provider locking does not show runtime scale decisions.

questions.learningObjective: Manage Terraform and runtime capacity together
questions.stem: Azure autoscale raises capacity above the module's desired default. What should be reviewed before a later Terraform apply?

options.A: Whether the plan proposes reconciling instances back to the configured value
options.B: Assume Terraform automatically ignores every capacity difference
options.C: Delete state to hide the autoscale decision
options.D: Remove all bounds so Terraform cannot see the scale set

optionExplanations.A: This module sets instances directly, so runtime capacity drift can appear in a plan.
optionExplanations.B: The module has no declared ignore_changes for instances.
optionExplanations.C: That loses tracking and can orphan resources.
optionExplanations.D: Bounds do not control Terraform's ability to read resources.

questions.stem: Should autoscale_capacity.default be interpreted as a guarantee that runtime capacity always equals that value?

options.A: Yes; autoscale settings never change capacity
options.B: Yes; only manual scaling can affect Windows VMSS
options.C: No; because the value is a password placeholder
options.D: No; active rules can move capacity within the minimum and maximum

optionExplanations.A: Changing capacity is the policy's purpose.
optionExplanations.B: Windows scale sets support configured autoscaling.
optionExplanations.C: It is a capacity count.
optionExplanations.D: Default is not a permanent fixed fleet size under autoscaling.

questions.stem: Autoscale is enabled while the shared VMSS upgrade policy remains Manual. What does autoscaling not guarantee?

options.A: That eligible new capacity changes can occur
options.B: That every existing instance has automatically received each later model or extension change
options.C: That the VMSS remains a valid Azure compute resource
options.D: That CPU can be measured

optionExplanations.A: That is the configured autoscale function.
optionExplanations.B: Capacity automation is distinct from model upgrade propagation.
optionExplanations.C: The setting does not invalidate the VMSS.
optionExplanations.D: CPU metrics are the rule's intended input.

questions.learningObjective: Improve operations for the bounded fleet
questions.stem: Which monitoring additions fit the lesson's production guidance?

options.A: Cost alerts, quota headroom, warm-up awareness, and operational dashboards
options.B: Only a permanent RDP source of 0.0.0.0/0
options.C: Only an administrator password displayed publicly
options.D: Only a weekly rename of every VMSS instance

optionExplanations.A: Bounds need supporting operations and evidence under changing demand.
optionExplanations.B: Broad management exposure does not monitor scaling.
optionExplanations.C: Secrets should not be used as dashboards.
optionExplanations.D: Naming churn does not improve capacity operations.

questions.stem: Why should the autoscale setting be removed before its target VMSS during cleanup?

options.A: The setting stores all Windows OS disks inside itself
options.B: The load balancer cannot be deleted while a browser quiz is open
options.C: The setting depends on the scale-set target resource ID
options.D: The minimum capacity prevents any resource from ever being destroyed

optionExplanations.A: OS disks are not stored in the autoscale setting.
optionExplanations.B: Browser state does not control Azure dependency deletion.
optionExplanations.C: Terraform's dependency graph supports removing dependent resources first.
optionExplanations.D: Destroy removes the policy and target rather than performing scale-in.

questions.learningObjective: Verify final absence rather than low demand
questions.stem: CPU falls to zero after testing. What is still needed for final CLZ-270 cleanup?

options.A: Only wait for autoscale to remove every billable resource
options.B: Destroy the managed resources and verify the captured group no longer exists
options.C: Only delete the saved quiz score
options.D: Only close the load-generating terminal

optionExplanations.A: The policy respects a minimum and does not clean up all services.
optionExplanations.B: Low demand does not delete the autoscale setting, minimum fleet, disks, or frontend.
optionExplanations.C: Learning progress does not remove Azure resources.
optionExplanations.D: Closing the client leaves the Azure footprint provisioned.
